title: Commits, Branches & Merge
objectives: Explain what a commit records and how the staging area shapes it
Choose correctly between fast-forward merges and merge commits
Write atomic commits with Conventional Commits messages
body:
# Commits, Branches & Merge

A bug "worked yesterday" and broke today, yet nobody can name the commit responsible. Diagnosing regressions, reviewing features, and rolling back mistakes all depend on readable history, and readable history starts with understanding what a commit really is.

## The problem

A repository without disciplined commits is an unsearchable pile of code. You cannot bisect a bug, review a feature, or revert a mistake when one commit mixes five unrelated edits. Teams need history that reads like a story: one purpose per commit, one line of development per idea.

## Constraints

- A commit is a full snapshot plus metadata: parent pointers, author, committer, timestamp, and message.
- The staging area (index) lets you compose exactly what the next commit contains.
- A branch is just a movable pointer to one commit, so creating one costs nothing.
- A merge either fast-forwards (linear history) or creates a merge commit with two parents.

## Options

- `git add -p`: stage hunk by hunk to keep commits atomic.
- `git switch -c feature/login`: isolate work on a branch that costs nothing.
- `git merge --ff-only main`: fast-forward when possible, refuse otherwise.
- `git merge --no-ff feature/login`: force a merge commit that documents the landing.
- Conventional Commits: `type(scope): summary`, e.g. `feat(auth): add login rate limiter`.

```bash
git switch -c feature/login
git add -p
git commit -m "feat(auth): add login rate limiter"
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature/login
```

## Tradeoffs

Fast-forward merges keep history linear and `git bisect`-friendly, but they erase the fact that a feature branch ever existed. Merge commits preserve that context and make feature-level rollbacks explicit, at the cost of a noisier graph. Atomic commits demand discipline up front and pay off in review and debugging; monolithic commits are fast to make and impossible to untangle later.

## Decision guide

Short-lived feature branches that go through review favor `--no-ff` (or squash) merges into `main`. A tiny local fix with no divergence can simply fast-forward. Never mix refactor and behavior change in one commit: if the message needs the word "and" twice, split it with `git add -p`. Prefer fast-forward for solo linear work and merge commits for anything that landed through review.

## Best practices

- Commit small and early: each commit should build, pass tests, and do one thing.
- Write imperative subject lines: "add rate limiter", not "added rate limiter".
- Use Conventional Commit types: feat, fix, docs, chore, refactor, test.
- Run `git status` and `git diff --staged` before every commit.
- Name branches after the task: `feature/GH-123-login-rate-limit`.

## Common mistakes

- `git commit -am "stuff"` bundling unrelated changes into one blob.
- Committing straight to `main` because branching felt like overhead.
- Expecting `git merge` to fast-forward after `main` has also moved.
- Ignoring the staging area, then losing hunks you meant to commit.
- Treating merge conflicts as failures instead of normal collaboration signals.

examples.name: Inspect before you commit
examples.code:
git status
git diff --staged
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -5

examples.name: Fast-forward vs merge commit
examples.code:
git merge --ff-only feature/login   # fails if main has diverged
git merge --no-ff feature/login     # always creates a merge commit

exercise.prompt: Simulate merge behavior as data. Each case records where main and feature point plus each commit's parent. Compute the verdict for merging feature into main and print one line per case: `case-a: fast-forward` or `case-b: merge commit required`.
hints: Follow the parent chain starting at the feature tip; if you ever reach the main commit, main is an ancestor.
If the chain ends without meeting main, the branches diverged and Git must create a merge commit.
Build one verdict string per case and join the lines with newlines.

questions.prompt: You touched three unrelated files and want one clean commit per logical change. Which command stages changes hunk by hunk?
questions.explanation: git add -p walks through each hunk so you can stage exactly one logical change per commit.

questions.prompt: main moved forward while feature/login was in progress. What does git merge feature/login produce on main?
options: A merge commit with two parents, because main has commits that feature does not
An automatic rebase of feature onto main
Nothing; Git refuses to merge diverged branches
questions.explanation: Once both branches have advanced, fast-forwarding is impossible, so Git records a merge commit whose parents are both branch tips.

questions.prompt: Which subject line follows Conventional Commits?
options: fixed login bugs and also updated deps
questions.explanation: Conventional Commits use type(scope): summary in the imperative mood, such as fix(auth): reject empty passwords.
